summary.qualitative: The candidate gets the headline shape right — the by-design home-trust finding and zsh wrapper, the $0.50 budget-cap failure and $1.00 re-run, the ~2.7s/~13s/$0.38 baseline numbers, the pivot to Jev turn-filtering, and the Jev cost arithmetic ($0.042/Mtok → ~$0.002/session) — and it observes the five-section structure with origin labels in D. It is far weaker than the reference on process detail and provenance: essentially all of the debugging texture (ugrep complexity error, illegal byte sequence, ToolSearch→curl fallback, script iterations), the knowledge-base grounding (working-conventions.md, headless-clean-agents.md, the 2026-08-02 "marks" case), the concrete design decisions (linux-ssh topic and #48/65 rationale, real config dir due to Keychain OAuth, ≤400-char rubric / 22.6k chars, arm-B bar, cold-read retargeting), and the entire aura-distill status answer (v1.1.17, 114 files, 99k words, SPINE 79/80) are absent. Its most serious defect is systematic misattribution: sections B, C and D repeatedly credit the user with facts, explanations and directives that were the assistant's own (TypeSafe/SPINE details, repo layout, topic choice, "update README", the separate-repo preference), and it invents user emotions and a "several hours" duration. Net: a thin but mostly readable skeleton with low recall and several confidently wrong actor/origin assignments.

Slightly loose: the backgrounded output was read and returned garbage, and further Python searches followed.
Garbled causality: the Jev arm is blocked on a missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY, not on the 'go' sequencing; 'go' triggered the baseline, which the assistant ran itself.
candidate_claims.reason: The unexecuted Jev arm and the 'go' go-ahead are both real; the causal link between them is garbled (the blocker is the missing API key).

candidate_claims.note: Cell-01 did not succeed — it was budget-exhausted and discarded; 3 valid cells plus 1 replacement.
candidate_claims.reason: The higher-budget replacement cell is real; 'all four succeeded' contradicts cell-01's budget exhaustion.

candidate_claims.note: Replacement text is exact but the edit was done with a Python string replace, not sed.
candidate_claims.reason: The README edit and its exact replacement text are real; the mechanism (Python string replace, not sed) is wrong.

candidate_claims.note: The budget failure and fix were entirely assistant-side; the user never mentioned it.
candidate_claims.reason: The budget-cap failure and $1 fix are real; classifying them as a user correction/teaching assigns the wrong actor.

candidate_claims.note: Wrong actor — the assistant discovered all three; the user asked what TypeSafe does.
candidate_claims.reason: TypeSafe details, SPINE layout and the ledger all appear in the transcript; the assistant discovered them, so the actor is wrong.

candidate_claims.note: Numbers are real (from docs/assistant arithmetic) but attributed to the user.
candidate_claims.reason: The $0.042/Mtok figure and the one-call-per-session reasoning are real; the actor is wrong (docs + assistant arithmetic).

candidate_claims.note: distill-process.md has 'Step 1: Identify signals'; 'exchanges' is the assistant's newly proposed unit, not part of the existing process.
candidate_claims.reason: 'Step 1: Identify signals' genuinely exists in distill-process.md; conflating it with the assistant's newly proposed 'exchanges' unit mis-states a real thing.

candidate_claims.note: The assistant proposed the split and explicitly asked the user; nothing was drafted.
candidate_claims.reason: A real repo-split proposal exists; the claim wrongly assigns the preference to the user and over-states progress ('started drafting').

candidate_claims.note: The assistant chose the repo location and the linux-ssh topic; the user only asked for a measurement.
candidate_claims.reason: Repo layout, topic choice and timing design all happened; wrong actor — the assistant made those calls.

candidate_claims.note: The cited commands were run by the assistant, not the user.
candidate_claims.reason: The cited commands genuinely occurred in the transcript; the actor is wrong (assistant ran them, not the user).

candidate_claims.note: The user never reacted to the cell failure; his only reaction was measured pragmatism about the 13s result.
candidate_claims.reason: No user reaction to the priced-out cell or to results exists anywhere; both frustration and excitement are invented emotional states.

candidate_claims.note: The cited explanations are the assistant's; the user's TypeSafe knowledge is contradicted by his request for a summary of what it does.
candidate_claims.reason: The detailed SPINE and distill-process explanations exist but are the assistant's; the attribution and the resulting expertise claim are wrong.

candidate_claims.note: The user asked for measurement but explicitly delegated the method ('your call'); the headless choice was the assistant's.
Origin is assistant preference, pending the user's answer — the user never expressed it.
candidate_claims.reason: The jev-distill-signals proposal is real; labelling it a decision with user-directive origin misattributes an assistant preference pending approval.

candidate_claims.note: The user never issued any README instruction.
candidate_claims.reason: Committing baseline results to the README really happened; the origin (a user 'update README' instruction) misattributes a real decision.

candidate_claims.note: Assistant-designed requirement from the TypeSafe docs; no user instruction.
candidate_claims.reason: The TYPESAFE_API_KEY requirement is real; its origin label (user directive) is wrong — it was assistant-designed from the docs.
